idiom_name: Servlet container lifecycle: init/service/destroy on HttpServlet
implementation_notes: The servlet container owns the component lifecycle: it loads and instantiates the servlet, calls init with the configuration before the first request, invokes service (and doGet/doPost) once per request, and calls destroy before taking the instance out of service - your code never drives that sequence. This is the classic framework-hook form and remains the right shape when a component needs container-managed resources and a stable per-instance lifecycle. Where the framework instead discovers annotated callbacks, that style is usually more concise.
pitfalls: The container calls service concurrently on one instance, so servlet fields must be immutable or thread-safe; per-request state belongs in local variables.
init must complete before requests are served and destroy only runs after in-flight requests finish (or a container timeout), so resource work there directly delays startup or shutdown.

variants.name: Annotation-driven container callbacks (Spring Boot, JUnit 5)
variants.idiom_name: annotation-driven container callbacks (Spring Boot ApplicationRunner, JUnit 5 lifecycle)
variants.implementation_notes: Modern Java frameworks invert control through annotations rather than explicit interfaces: Spring Boot calls @PostConstruct and ApplicationRunner.run at defined points in startup, and JUnit 5 discovers and invokes @BeforeEach/@AfterEach/@Test methods on your class. This replaces the hand-written interface implementation with metadata - the dominant style in application code - but moves the call graph out of the source. Implement the interface directly when ordering, typed arguments or an explicit contract matter more than brevity.
pitfalls: Annotation-discovered hooks run in a framework-defined order that is invisible at the call site; relying on the order of several runners or @BeforeEach methods is a classic source of flakiness.
Reflection-based invocation wraps failures in framework exceptions and may skip later lifecycle phases, so the phase and original cause must be read from the framework's report.
